Hey all, I have been working on a formalization of "A general lower bound on the number of examples needed for learning" (Ehrenfeucht et al., 1989) in my fork of Cslib and hoping to make a PR pretty soon with the PAC framework and lower bounds. The lower bound is proved (theorem 1 from the paper), but I am trying to get things into a nice shape for review now and probably squash some of the commits, as there are quite a few by now.

Opening up a thread now in case folks want to chat about it. I am doing it to learn this paper better and practice with the Mathlib measure theory interfaces, as I read it in college but it's been a long time. It would be really cool if anyone wanted to implement some upper bounds.
I think I'll topsort the modules I wound up with and make commits corresponding to that such that it can be reviewed commit by commit, that sounds like a sane approach.
Here's the PR: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/483

Is the silence here implicitly saying "this work is not wanted here", or is it suggesting nobody is currently interested in reviewing? I am working on more machine learning stuff today, formalizing the results about vanishing gradients from the 90s to the 2010s ending with ResNet, showing that residual networks don't have the same vanishing gradient issues under random initialization.
I think reviewer capacity is stretched thin on the official side. Afaik I am qualified to review this. But it’s also a lot to review in one go
I can’t even run the CI which is usually my sanity check.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

I think reviewer capacity is stretched thin on the official side. Afaik I am qualified to review this. But it’s also a lot to review in one go

Yes, silence is more this than anything else. I'm especially busy this month and Fabrizio is travelling as well. If you see no activity over something like a week or two, please ping me so I can at least try to assign the review to someone.

We appreciate the patience as we're in the very early stages of expanding "official" reviewers. As a reminder anyone, especially if they feel they have domain expertise, is encouraged to leave reviews.
Fwiw i wrote a masters thesis and taught in a reading group on this topic

And I have an ongoing research collab around it. So technically I can review it. I still prefer smaller PRs. For instance I think PAC learning models are the most obvious use case of queries. The Kearns and Vazirani book literally frames it this way if memory serves me right.

It would be helpful if there was a way to run CI. I am currently working on my definitions of these models. I’d like to see an initial PR which contains the following definitions.
1.PAC learning.

  1. Noisy pac learning
  2. Agnostic PAC learning.

All for binary classification.

As I've explained somewhere before, the CI not running automatically is a security default that GitHub has for the first PR by a new contributor that I don't think there is a quick workaround for. You can still run everything locally.
So it sounds like I should just wait for reviews on the PR for now. Happy to respond to any comments there :)

Hi, Dhruv here. Shreyas and Samuel pointed me to this thread.
I have a Lean 4 repo formalizing results in statistical learning theory, including the fundamental theorem, PAC characterization (VC <-> PAC biconditional), sample complexity bounds (upper via symmetrization, lower via shattering), compression with side information (Moran-Yehudayoff), and some other results (Littlestone, Gold, PAC-Bayes).

Repo: https://github.com/Zetetic-Dhruv/formal-learning-theory-kernel
I have explained more details here  .

I would love to contribute to learning theory from this repo in any way I can. Let me know if and how I can contribute here.
From my end, I'm just finding that repository pretty noisy and hard to review holistically. There is a lot there. Is there a specific theorem you'd like help reviewing by any chance?

I was travelling; it looks relevant! As already pointed out, it would be very helpful to split into smaller PRs, if possible.
Glad for the confirmation! I'll split out the first definitions PR when I get the chance.

Here's the definitions PR: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/492.

@Dhruv Gupta I'd love to get your feedback, as I intended for this to be compatible with your definitions as well. It generalizes from sets to distributions, which ended up being decently ergonomic.

This PR is a substantial improvement over the previous PR. But I still have some suggestions here

  1. You probably shouldn’t take up the machine learning namespace. Maybe MLTheory is better.

  2. Your current notion of “learning protocol” only covers passive batch learning scenarios. There are active learning models. And there are adversarial sampler models. There are also teaching models. The ideal learning theory framework would cover all these models using a notion of a learner learning from an oracle. The oracle is a separate entity. We will need to give it distinct semantics for distinct oracle models. PAC learning is a special case of this where the oracle just obeys a probability distribution not known to the learner, but only to the oracle.

The definition I am suggesting is the closest to a “most general definition” in this area. Naturally we want this because sample complexity and related API needn’t be repeated for each variant

How about we call it "batch learning" or "non-adaptive learning" then? I think there is value in having this specialized API, as there are theorems you can prove here that aren't as easy to prove in the adaptive setting.
We definitely need specific theorems for specific variants like adaptive/batch learning.
But I am first trying to pin down the most general notions of learning theory.
I thought we were going for PAC learning specifically here?

I feel like having "the most general learning theory" thing is a nice thing we can do once we have several examples of ergonomic proofs within specific subdomains, but not necessary to get started in this area. I've already generalized quite substantially and we'll be able to prove a lot of interesting theorems with these definitions.

The analogy I have in my head is for Lambda Calculus and Pure Type Systems. We could define a global Pure Type System for a wide variety of lambda calculi, including the untyped lambda calculus. But we don't, we have a number of specialized ones.
Actually @Chris Henson is trying to make it all unified.
We had a similar effort for LTSes earlier this year.
I have also explored this, I think its a good idea!
But I don't think it blocked these things from entering the codebase to begin proving interesting things and iterating :)
We can merge this simpler notion of PAC learning and then generalize later, is my argument.
If we didn’t know how to generalise I would agree.
This was the scenario in LTSes
But here we do know how to build modular and general definitions.
We knew how to do it for Lambda Calculi, pure type systems have been around for decades.
Anyways, so you'd prefer to wait on adding the PAC learning definitions until we have the oracle interaction model from Algolean I am guessing.

I think there are the following moving pieces in all learning setups.

  1. The learner, who queries an oracle (data set/distribhtion/active teacher/constrained adversarial teacher) for one or more samples and one or more times, including sometimes proposing a hypotheses to this oracle. It finally outputs a hypothesis.
  2. The oracle’s interface. This is how the oracle lets the learner interact with it.
  3. The semantics of the oracle.
  4. The cost and complexity measures (sample, time, and even space).
  5. Measures of error/ loss functions.
The ideal definition will set this up and establish various pac learning models as special cases of this general setup.
Yes, this is reasonable. We don't have a lot of these tools set up very well already, which is why I focused on proving the information theoretic lower bound based on VC dimension :)
Whatever setup we use to establish these definitions in the end is less important. The more important thing is we don’t repeat ourselves when defining these things for each model.
Fwiw the crypto protocols people are also using a similar free monad idea.
I am also using one for my proof of Fiat-Shamir's security in the ROM.

I'm familiar with the technique of using free monads for oracle interaction, here's my version: https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/cslib/blob/main/Cslib/Cryptography/Foundations/OracleInteraction.lean

I'm not arguing against that long term. I'm just arguing we shouldn't hold up PAC learning and the VC-based lower bounds because we haven't agreed on this interface yet. And when we define this interface, we should port PAC learning to rely on it.
I’ll let the official reviewers and maintainers chime in on that. I have laid out how to achieve mathlib style generality in this area.
I think this is an example of letting perfect be the enemy of the good, but I am also curious about what the reviewers think.
Normally I’d agree but we really ought to avoid building a bazaar and instead build a cathedral from the beginning when possible. Once the library grows to a certain point, refactors become costly.

One thing I am still skeptical about is using FinVecs for learning samples. The reason is you have to introduce a Nat index into your type and now there is an artificial separation between the types of different samples and learning algorithms depending on m
Which means a bunch of set/list like operations that appear in learning theory proofs might suddenly become complicated.
Definitely open to using Lists if that is preferred, it doesn't change much cause I can just turn it to a FinVec whenever I want to use that API.

build a cathedral from the beginning

I definitely believe in this too. To me, this means ensuring that our work is compatible with generalizations such that generalizing will be simple in the future. I believe this is the case here.

I am unusually busy this week (a talk and an interview) but will definitely take a look as soon as possible. Thank you for the separate PR to make it easier to start reviewing.

I will say that the pure type system analogy is one I empathize with. I think I've only ever seen one formalization that took this route, and even then it isn't very ergonomic and doesn't generalize to more complex type systems. We'll of course do our best to pick the right abstractions, but my impression is that this can be particularly difficult for CS formalization. So thanks for the patience as we review, we are appreciative of your time and interest in adding these new areas to CSLib.

To clarify. The 4 part split I am suggesting comes from my experience in the area. We often relate models and jump across them. So it is useful to have a definition which allows this.

In fact consider the textbook (kearns and vazirani) proof that PAC learning 3 DNFs is NP Hard. Here you already need to mix sampling oracles with computational oracles.

Another point. It is a sign of insufficient generality that there needs to be two different sample complexity definitions. Sample complexity is a single idea that spans common passive learning models.

We could do something like

  abbrev LearnerModel (α β : Type*) [MeasurableSpace α] [MeasurableSpace β] :=
    ℕ → Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ≥0) 1 → Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ≥0) 1 →
      ConceptClass α β → Set (Measure (α × β)) → Prop

  noncomputable def sampleComplexity (L : LearnerModel α β)
      (C : ConceptClass α β) (ε δ : Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ≥0) 1)
      (𝒟 : Set (Measure (α × β))) : ℕ :=
    sInf {m : ℕ | L m ε δ C 𝒟}

instead. Then we could instantiate LearnerModel with IsPACLearnerFor C ε δ 𝒟 and IsRPACLearnerFor C ε δ 𝒟 if you'd like.
Correction to my previous message : sample complexity also applies to active and teaching models. Just the ones which aren’t allowed other queries. Those have sample and the other query complexities.
Yes, I agree. Though if we agree to define the batch learning setting here then we can defer those to when we generalize. That is the debate, after all :)
Yes, but I am guessing you do see that with a general approach we have one definition and API for sample complexity rather than several (meaning one set of grind and simp lemmas)
I don't think so, I believe we'll end up wanting specialized lemmata for the passive case for several reasons, even if they're proven to be equivalent to the general case.
My view is we'll end up proving the equivalence of the active case to the passive case under specific circumstances, but we'll still want definitions quite close to mine for proving against.
This is why I believe there is fundamentally no cost to what we're doing there. I'd love to see a PR which proved me wrong tbh.
I could easily be convinced if you showed me how to do it better, then I'd happily write my proofs against that code.
that's a tall ask. I am saying you could improve things in this very PR. To be upfront I have reasons for writing this PAC learning stuff in my model, but that code is private for now.

Oh, perhaps I am confused. How can I improve things with the machinery we currently have in Cslib in this PR? Do you want me to define a monad and a semantics for it for sampling tuples from the measure?
If you did that you would be reinventing my RandomSample oracle
I mean, that's why I asked you to submit a PR to cslib :)
cslib#372 has existed for a while
I would have to write my PR on top of it, which would create 1700 line diffs
I'll let relevant decisions be made first.
Thanks for context

Hi,
I had a conversation with Samuel. I will be contributing to his sample complexity PR
After reading the current thread, I agree with Shreyas on his propositions but in context of interactive learning theory.
In passive statistical learning theory, the oracle layer is very simple (single sampling primitive) and PAC characterization foundations, including the sample complexity definitions and bounds, do not require interactive interfaces..
I think Samuel's current PR is not blocked by the oracle layer and at the same time, any interactive learning theory proofs (very interesting in their own right) will certainly need it. I think we should discuss that in a separate topic.

Dhruv Gupta said:

In passive statistical learning theory, the oracle layer is very simple (single sampling primitive) and PAC foundations, including the sample complexity definitions and bounds, do not require interactive interfaces..

  1. They do. Especially when you want to prove textbook NP Hardness theorems.
  2. You'd be repeating the sample complexity API unnecessarily.

I have no opinions on this PR per se, since I intend to pursue my own definitions in Algolean that are more unified, and thus better API. I am battle-testing them on a presently open problem for now. If this PR offers theorems I can reuse then I'd probablly use those.

My perspective is that we should have both things in Cslib. In particular, proving PAC learning 3-DNFs is NP-hard is great. Even if we had the oracle-based free monad like you've suggested and I vaguely agree with (though I'd need to see a PR to agree on specifics), we would still have definitions like the one I proposed to prove the VC-dimension sample complexity lower bound, given that this (actually, the original PR's definition, which I'll end up specializing to again in proof code) is the property they're proving against in their proofs.

One small nitpick about references. The Kearns and Vazirani book is 3 decades old and later textbooks have improved the way definitions are presented. We taught in our reading course with the Mohri et al book. I think the Shai Shalev Schwartz and Shai Ben David book has an even better ordering and presentation of definitions. Since one purpose served (perhaps unofficially) by references is to refer contributors to books we recommend using, I suggest referring to one or both of these books.
Please leave a comment on the PR Shreyas, it is easier to keep track of the PR feedback there.
If you don't mind, could you also tell me the difference in the definitions in those books, cause I only have the Kearns and Vazirani one.

The books are freely available on the authors webpages

  1. https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~shais/UnderstandingMachineLearning/understanding-machine-learning-theory-algorithms.pdf

  2. https://cs.nyu.edu/~mohri/mlbook/

1 defines loss functions from the get go. 2 uses more familiar modern terminology and specializes definitions to the binary case. Both also deal with multi class classification and regression. By using them you get consistent terminology and notation for the entire area. This is simply a consequence of the fact that Kearns and Vazirani appeared two decades before these books and a lot of literature in this field.
